title: Digital ID and what it would be used for

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: The digital ID proposal is back. One credential on your phone for tax, health, right to work, the lot.

turns.speaker: Gemma
turns.text: Estonia's run something like that for twenty years and it's genuinely popular there.

turns.speaker: Idris
turns.text: Estonia also built it alongside a law that logs every official access and lets you see who looked at your record.

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: That's the part that never makes it into the copy.

turns.speaker: Idris
turns.text: It's the whole thing, though. The card isn't the policy. The accountability around it is the policy.

turns.speaker: Gemma
turns.text: The convenience case is real, mind you. Proving who you are currently means a utility bill and a passport photocopy, which is absurd in itself and also easy to forge.

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: And it's worst for people who move often or have no bank account.

turns.speaker: Gemma
turns.text: Which is the group usually invoked against it and is arguably helped most by it.

turns.speaker: Idris
turns.text: My objection isn't the database, it's function creep. It arrives for tax and within a decade you need it to rent a flat.

turns.speaker: Ken
turns.text: That has happened elsewhere, to be fair.

turns.speaker: Idris
turns.text: Repeatedly. Nobody ever announces it. Each extension is small and sensible.

turns.speaker: Gemma
turns.text: So legislate the list of uses and require a vote to add one.

turns.speaker: Idris
turns.text: That I could support. What I won't support is trusting a promise that it stays narrow.

points: A digital ID proposal would combine tax, health and right-to-work credentials.
Gemma cites Estonia's long-running and popular system.
Idris notes Estonia paired it with laws logging every official access and letting citizens see who viewed their record, which he considers the substance of the policy.
The convenience case is strong, since current identity checks rely on forgeable documents and disadvantage people who move often or lack bank accounts.
Idris's main objection is function creep, where narrow uses expand incrementally without announcement.
They agree a legislated list of permitted uses, requiring a vote to extend, would address the concern better than assurances.
